messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos Morales was forty, a seasoned laparoscopic surgeon whose hands moved with surgical precision and confidence. On a humid July morning, while preparing for a routine cholecystectomy in the West Wing of St. Vincent’s, the world around him erupted into a cacophony of terror. An earthquake of magnitude 7.2 struck the city, sending the entire building into violent oscillation. The fluorescent lights flickered, and a thunderous roar rolled over the hallways as the HVAC system groaned. The air grew thick with a metallic tang and the acrid scent of burning plastic as a corridor burned. In the chaos, a steel support column fell, crushing a stretcher and sending sparks into the ceiling. Carlos felt the ground shift under his feet and heard the distant wail of ambulance sirens, the sound that now cuts through his consciousness like a knife. The sheer intensity of that day’s auditory, olfactory, and visual assault left Carlos with a fractured memory. He tells the therapist that a simple clatter of a coffee cup or the hiss of a fire alarm can suddenly plunge him back into that moment. The trigger of a loud noise immediately conjures the jarring crash of the support column, while a faint whiff of smoke or burnt plastic takes him straight to the burning corridor. In that flash, he sees his colleagues’ faces, the twisted metal, the smoke, the sound of distant sirens, yet he is also aware that the picture is incomplete – a half-remembered jigsaw that never fully resolves. When he recalls the disaster, an overwhelming wave of grief washes over him, and he becomes haunted by the fact that he could not save everyone. In the days and weeks that followed, these triggers spiraled into a cycle of maladaptive coping. The siren’s wail at the start of a night shift forced Carlos to pull out a bottle of whiskey from the kitchen cabinet, his fingers trembling as he poured a quick drink. The smell of smoke that seeped through the ventilation system made him think of the burnt corridor, and he turned to sexual fantasies to distract his mind from the looming threat. The noise of the hospital’s patient monitors, a low-frequency hum that felt like the tremors of the earthquake, compelled him to play loud music on his phone, a form of auditory distraction that momentarily pulled him out of the memory. He would also mentally sprint through a surgical procedure, rehearsing incisions, to occupy the space left by the disaster. Each of these strategies was an attempt to quell the panic that surged when a trigger resurfaced, yet they only deepened the gap in his memory, reinforcing the feeling that he could not fully remember what happened. The interlocking relationships among triggers, memory, and maladaptive strategies became clearer as Carlos’s behavior changed. In the second half of his recovery, the memory of the disaster—its incomplete fragments and grief—fed back into his sensitivity to triggers. When he heard the ambulance siren, he instantly remembered the building’s collapse, and that recollection would, in turn, prompt him to drink or indulge in fantasy. The same pattern applied when the smell of smoke drifted through the cafeteria; the memory of the burned corridor surged, pushing him toward distraction or alcohol. Each maladaptive strategy, while temporarily soothing, reinforced the disjointedness of his memory, creating a tightening loop that left Carlos feeling trapped in a perpetual state of hyperarousal. The practical consequences of this cycle are evident in Carlos’s professional life. He has begun arriving late for morning rounds, skipping the pre-operative briefing to avoid the sound of the hospital’s alarm system. He reports that colleagues have noticed his guarded demeanor, and his wife has expressed concern about his increasing isolation. At home, the quiet night is no longer a sanctuary; the quiet can feel like a void ready to be filled with the echo of distant sirens, and he finds himself drinking to avoid the intrusive images. The weight of these symptoms finally pushed Carlos to seek help. He is haunted by the thought that he might never regain the full picture of that day, and he fears that the cycle will keep him from fully living in the present. Yet he also hopes that, with therapy, he can break the loop and find a way to honor the memory without allowing it to control his life.
